title: Beyond the Die: Verifying the Connected Chip
gist: A TSMC OIP Forum presentation by Siemens EDA, Marvell and TSMC describes automated reliability and ESD verification of assembled 3D IC CoWoS systems using Calibre PERC and Calibre 3D PERC. Chiplet integration makes verification a system-level problem, replacing a manual flow of two to three weeks.

insights.claim: In multidie assemblies, individual die qualification cannot substitute for checking the assembled protection network, because the structure protecting a circuit may sit on another die with a different protection scheme and process.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging complexity expands verification scope and demand for assembly-level EDA tools.
insights.locator: Electrostatic discharge, or ESD, illustrates the problem

insights.claim: Dividing a design across dies in TSMC CoWoS creates new dependencies: electrical connections now extend through dies, bumps, interposers and substrates, so a part that passes its own checks may be unsafe once assembled.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Chiplet adoption raises integration risk, favoring vendors with system-level verification flows.
insights.locator: But dividing a design creates new dependencies

insights.claim: SemiWiki has published more than 150 blogs on 3D IC over three years and expects to publish twice that many over the next three as chiplet adoption accelerates.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Editorial signal that chiplet and 3D IC activity is accelerating.

insights.claim: The methodology checks each die with Siemens Calibre PERC and foundry rule decks, then uses assembly information for Calibre 3D PERC checks across the integrated system.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Extends Siemens' installed Calibre base into 3D IC, supporting its position in advanced-packaging sign-off.

insights.claim: The checks cover three areas: protection topology, point-to-point resistance and current density.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Defines the checklist advanced-package ESD sign-off requires.

insights.claim: The earlier workflow of separate die checks, manual interface verification and manual debugging could take two to three weeks; the transcript gives no measured replacement runtime.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Productivity gain is asserted but unquantified; treat the benefit claim cautiously.
insights.locator: The speakers describe an earlier workflow

insights.claim: Scale makes automation essential: one package ball can connect through multiple bumps and branches, producing many paths, and engineers need debugging tools showing which layers or connections cause a violation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Computational load and debug tooling are differentiators among EDA vendors for 3D IC.

themes.theme: Why integration risk matters for AI

insights.claim: AI infrastructure depends on advanced packaging, which concentrates value and risk within each assembly, so one protection failure can compromise a package of otherwise functional dies.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging-level failures are a yield and cost risk for AI accelerators; this supports verification spend.
insights.locator: Why this matters extends beyond verification productivity

insights.claim: Ten components each with a 99 percent success probability combine to roughly 90 percent, assuming independence; the presentation uses this as an illustration of compounding risk, not a yield prediction.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Compounding risk gives a mental model for why multi-die packages need early integration checks.

insights.claim: Reliability and ESD specialists should participate from the beginning of the design, with rules matched to the assembly and visibility across component boundaries.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Shift-left verification: finding integration problems before fabrication prevents costly redesigns and schedule slips.
insights.quote: As chips become systems, verification must follow.
